{{Short description|Formula for the sum of an arithmetic function}}
In [[mathematics]], and more particularly in [[analytic number theory]], '''Perron's formula''' is a formula discovered by [[Oskar Perron]] to calculate the sum of an [[arithmetic function]], by means of an inverse [[Mellin transform]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Perron |first1=Oskar |title=Zur Theorie der Dirichletschen Reihen |trans-title=On the theory of Dirichlet series |journal=Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik (Crelles Journal) |date=1 July 1908 |volume=1908 |issue=134 |pages=95–143 |doi=10.1515/crll.1908.134.95 |url=https://eudml.org/doc/149285 |access-date=8 March 2026 |language=German}}</ref>

==Statement==
Let <math>\{a(n)\}</math> be an [[arithmetic function]], and let

<math display="block"> g(s)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{a(n)}{n^{s}}</math>
 
be the corresponding [[Dirichlet series]]. Presume the Dirichlet series to be [[uniform convergence|uniformly convergent]] for <math>\Re(s)>\sigma</math>. Then Perron's formula is

<math display="block"> A(x) = {\sum_{n\le x}}' a(n) =\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty} g(z)\frac{x^{z}}{z} \,dz.</math>

Here, the prime on the summation indicates that the last term of the sum must be multiplied by 1/2 when ''x'' is an [[integer]]. The integral is not a convergent [[Lebesgue integral]]; it is understood as the [[Cauchy principal value]]. The formula requires that ''c'' > 0, ''c'' > σ, and ''x'' > 0.

==Proof==
An easy sketch of the proof comes from taking [[Abel's summation formula|Abel's sum formula]]

<math display="block"> g(s)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{a(n)}{n^{s} }=s\int_{1}^{\infty}  A(x)x^{-(s+1) } dx. </math>

This is nothing but a [[Laplace transform]] under the variable change <math>x = e^t.</math> Inverting it one gets Perron's formula.

Proofs of Perron's formula have been published by [[Tom M. Apostol]]<ref>{{cite book |last1=Apostol |first1=Tom M. |title=Introduction to analytic number theory |date=1976 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=New York |isbn=978-0-387-90163-3 |pages=243–246 |mr=0434929 |zbl=0335.10001 }}</ref> and by [[Gérald Tenenbaum]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Tenenbaum |first1=Gérald |title=Introduction to analytic and probabilistic number theory |date=1995 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge; New York |series=Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics |volume=46 |isbn=0-521-41261-7 |pages=130–134 |zbl=0831.11001}}</ref>

==Examples==
Because of its general relationship to Dirichlet series, the formula is commonly applied to many number-theoretic sums. Thus, for example, one has the famous integral representation for the [[Riemann zeta function]]:

<math display="block">\zeta(s)=s\int_1^\infty \frac{\lfloor x\rfloor}{x^{s+1}}\,dx</math>

and a similar formula for [[Dirichlet L-function|Dirichlet ''L''-functions]]:

<math display="block">L(s,\chi)=s\int_1^\infty \frac{A(x)}{x^{s+1}}\,dx</math>

where

<math display="block">A(x)=\sum_{n\le x} \chi(n)</math>

and <math>\chi(n)</math> is a [[Dirichlet character]]. Other examples appear in the articles on the [[Mertens function]] and the [[von Mangoldt function]].

==Generalizations==

Perron's formula is a special case of the formula

<math display="block"> \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a(n)f(n/x)= \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}F(s)G(s)x^{s}ds </math>

where

<math display="block">G(s)= \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{a(n)}{n^{s}} </math>

and

<math display="block"> F(s)= \int_{0}^{\infty}f(x)x^{s-1}dx </math>

the Mellin transform. The Perron formula is the special case of the test function <math>f(1/x)=\theta (x-1),</math> for <math> \theta(x) </math> the [[Heaviside step function]].
